title: T1583.002 — Acquire Infrastructure - DNS Server
subtitle: Watch the full fast-flux story play out: setup, rotation, abuse, and the SOC answer.
aria: Animated diagram: an attacker registers a domain, runs an authoritative DNS server with fast-flux A and NS records, a victim resolves changing IPs and reaches C2 through flux nodes, and the SOC detects the flux and blocks the domain.

nodes.label: Attacker
nodes.tip: Registers the domain, rents the VPS nodes, and controls the DNS zone.

nodes.label: Auth DNS
nodes.tip: The attacker-run authoritative nameserver that answers for the zone with a 60-second TTL.

nodes.label: Flux node A
nodes.tip: Cheap rented server that serves payloads or C2 while its IP is in rotation.

nodes.label: Flux node B
nodes.tip: Second rotating node; answers alternate between the two IPs.

nodes.label: Victim
nodes.tip: Internal workstation that resolves the flux name and connects to whichever IP answered.

nodes.label: Resolver
nodes.tip: The internal recursive resolver; its logs are the best place to spot flux.

nodes.label: SOC
nodes.tip: Security operations center watching passive DNS and resolver telemetry.

steps.title: Register and rent
steps.caption: The attacker registers a domain and rents two cheap VPS nodes. The domain will soon answer for both servers.
steps.defender: Nothing is visible inside the estate yet. The only early clue sits outside: a fresh domain registration with unknown nameservers.

steps.title: Install DNS, TTL 60
steps.caption: The attacker installs authoritative DNS software and sets the TTL to 60 seconds, so old answers expire fast.
steps.defender: A new zone now exists on a young domain. Passive DNS vendors record its first NS records.

steps.title: IP flux
steps.caption: The attacker rotates the A records across both nodes. One name now points at many IP addresses that change every minute.
steps.defender: Passive DNS starts to show high IP cardinality: one parent domain, many answers, short TTL.

steps.title: NS flux
steps.caption: The attacker also rotates the nameserver records themselves, so even the who-answers-this-zone layer keeps moving.
steps.defender: The NS history of the domain changes several times a day. Churn at NS level is rare for normal sites.

steps.title: Victim resolves
steps.caption: The victim resolves the name again and again and gets a different IP each time, because the TTL is only 60 seconds.
steps.defender: Resolver logs show the same parent domain answered by different IPs for one client within minutes.

steps.title: Payload and C2
steps.caption: The payload download and the C2 (command and control) traffic go through whichever flux node answered last.
steps.defender: Egress logs show one internal host connecting to many short-lived IPs on the same name and port.

steps.title: SOC spots flux
steps.caption: The SOC passive DNS system counts the answers: high IP cardinality, a 60-second TTL, and constant NS churn for one domain.
steps.defender: A flux-detection alert fires. Triage: confirm the cardinality, check which clients queried the name, then prepare a resolver block.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: Block and report
steps.caption: The SOC blocks the domain at the resolver and reports the nameservers to the hosting provider for abuse.
steps.defender: Clients can no longer resolve the name. Watch for re-delegation: the same domain may return on new nameservers.
